solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

indicatorNotes.built: the letters of CLUB I are assembled into a new structure, as a builder does with bricks

blocks.note: a repertory theatre is a rep

annotation.surface: A national theatre company putting together a new club.
annotation.walkthrough: "State" reads as a verb, as if announcing something; it is the noun, a country without a monarch.
annotation.definitionFit: A republic is a state governed without a monarch.

entries.clue: Demand and obtain energy by law (5)

blocks.note: E is the physics symbol for energy
in arithmetic, 3 by 4 is written 3 x 4
an Act of Parliament is a law

annotation.surface: A tax officer extracting fuel payments under statutory powers.
annotation.walkthrough: "By" is the multiplication sign X, as in a room measuring ten feet by twelve.
annotation.definitionFit: To exact something is to demand it and get it, as in exacting a fee or revenge.

blocks.note: the London Tube is its railway system
think of coffee beans that have been milled too coarsely: split the answer as UNDER + a past participle

annotation.surface: A complaint that a tube is not quite fine enough for its purpose.
annotation.walkthrough: The Tube is London's underground railway. Read as UNDER-GROUND, the word describes coffee or flour that has not been ground finely enough.
annotation.definitionFit: The Tube is the popular name for the London Underground.

entries.clue: Making Fellow of poet not seen for ages (4-4)

blocks.note: the poet is Henry Wadsworth Longfellow; ask what must happen to his name to leave just FELLOW
a straight description of a relative or friend who has been missing for years

annotation.surface: A college electing a poet to a fellowship after he had vanished for years.
annotation.walkthrough: Read as an instruction, LONG LOST says: remove LONG from LONGFELLOW, and what is left is "Fellow". The capital F on Fellow is surface only.
annotation.definitionFit: Long-lost describes someone or something not seen for a very long time.

entries.clue: Critic one can see exploding bogus theory (8,7)

indicatorNotes.exploding: the fodder blows apart and its letters land in a new order

annotation.surface: A critic who can see a phoney theory being blown apart.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole run "Critic one can see" is the fodder; a critic exploding a theory is exactly what the surface expects, which hides the indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: Creation science claims scientific backing for the Genesis account of creation; the setter calls it a bogus theory.

annotation.surface: A call to free a single French composer.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a French composer such as Ravel; the composer is the American John Cage, and French only supplies UN.
annotation.definitionFit: To uncage is to set free from a cage, so to liberate.

entries.clue: Winning F1 driver we hear drank beer all over the place (2,4,4,4)

indicatorNotes.we hear: the next words are to be taken by their sound

blocks.note: a team that is winning is up
Graham Hill and his son Damon were both Formula One world champions
drank = downed, beer = ale; said together, the D slides across the gap

annotation.surface: A victorious racing driver celebrating by throwing beer everywhere.
annotation.walkthrough: Champagne-spraying winners make "all over the place" look like part of the scene; it is the definition. Downed ale and down dale sound the same.
annotation.definitionFit: Up hill and down dale means everywhere, in all directions.

indicatorNotes.oddly missing: the letters in odd places are the ones kept, and the rest go missing

annotation.surface: Someone preaching about a fungus, with bits of the sermon missing.
annotation.walkthrough: "Preach about" looks like a phrase meaning sermonise on a topic; "about" is the reversal indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: The cep is the edible porcino mushroom, a fungus.

entries.clue: Thin soup with fish is hard to get through (9)

annotation.surface: A meal of thin soup and fish that is a struggle to finish.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes "hard to get through" about eating a grim meal; it is the definition of an exhausting ordeal.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a gruelling task is an exhausting ordeal, one you struggle to get through.

blocks.note: par is the standard score in golf
to don is to put on or dress in

annotation.surface: Someone asking in what they are expected to dress for a formal occasion.
annotation.walkthrough: "What?" is the definition, the polite request to repeat something. "Dress in" is the surface phrase, but only "dress" gives DON.
annotation.definitionFit: "Pardon?" is a politer way of saying "what?" when you did not hear.

entries.clue: Prehistoric animal expert, on holiday in Paris, purchases unusual shrunken heads (8)

indicatorNotes.heads: take the head, the first letter, of each word

blocks.clueFragment: expert, on holiday in Paris, purchases unusual shrunken
blocks.note: the first letter of each of eight words

annotation.surface: A palaeontologist on holiday in Paris buying odd shrunken heads as souvenirs.
annotation.walkthrough: Shrunken heads sound like the souvenir; "heads" is the instruction to take initial letters of the eight preceding words.
annotation.definitionFit: Eohippus, the dawn horse, is an extinct early ancestor of the horse.

indicatorNotes.mostly cleared: most of the word is cleared out, leaving only its two ends

blocks.note: keep the first two and last two letters, clearing out ENHOUSEMU

annotation.surface: A jail in the Scottish town of Stenhousemuir that has been largely emptied.
annotation.walkthrough: Stenhousemuir is a small town in Scotland, best known for its football club. Stir is slang for prison.
annotation.definitionFit: Stir is old slang for prison, as in doing time in stir.

entries.clue: Hooters going off till we lost (6,4)

indicatorNotes.going off: the letters go off, like milk, into a new state

annotation.surface: Horns sounding off at the till because a team lost.
annotation.walkthrough: "Hooters" suggests horns or sirens going off; here hooters are birds that hoot.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the little owl is a small European owl species, and anything that hoots can be called a hooter.

entries.clue: Out in the open, bird keeps low – I’m delighted (4,3,4)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition includes "I'm" because the phrase is an adjective: "I'm over the moon" and "I'm delighted" swap exactly, and the setter defines the whole statement.

indicatorNotes.keeps: the bird holds the next piece inside it

blocks.note: to low is to moo like a cow

annotation.surface: A bird out in the open, keeping its voice down, and someone thrilled about it.
annotation.walkthrough: "Low" looks like an adjective, as in keeping a low profile; it is the verb for a cow's call.
annotation.definitionFit: Over the moon means extremely pleased.

entries.clue: Strange person (not working) sometimes ceases to drink (8)

indicatorNotes.not working: ON means working, so remove ON
indicatorNotes.sometimes: only some of the letters are used, every other one

blocks.note: the word itself, before anything is taken away
a machine that is working is on; "not" says these two letters are taken away, leaving PERS
second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

annotation.surface: An odd unemployed person who occasionally gives up drinking.
annotation.walkthrough: "Ceases to drink" reads as giving up alcohol, but the words split: "ceases to" is fodder and "drink" alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: An espresso is a strong black coffee, a drink.

annotation.surface: Economic measures that fail on the American stock exchange.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is financial, with flops on a stock exchange; "exchange" is the anagram indicator and "Measures" are kitchen quantities.
annotation.definitionFit: Spoonfuls are measures of quantity, as in two spoonfuls of sugar.

entries.clue: Lake where exclusive circle get rid of bed (4)

indicatorNotes.get rid of: remove the bed from the circle

annotation.surface: A lakeside resort where a snobbish set throw out a bed.
annotation.walkthrough: COTERIE loses its COT to leave one of the North American Great Lakes.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Erie is one of the five Great Lakes on the border of the USA and Canada.

indicatorNotes.Some: only some of the letters of the following words are used, in a consecutive run

blocks.note: the letters run across the word breaks

annotation.surface: Leftovers of an unappealing meal.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface invites a sneer at tofu itself; the answer is hidden across "remnant of unappetising".
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: bean curd pressed from soya milk is one kind of food among many.

indicatorNotes.to open: the identification goes into the beach, opening it up

annotation.surface: Needing ID before a beach will open to you.
annotation.walkthrough: "Want" reads as a verb; it is the noun meaning lack.
annotation.definitionFit: Want as a noun means lack, a shortage.

annotation.surface: Racists being told to leave in disgrace.
annotation.walkthrough: "Maybe" marks racists as one example of bigots, not the only kind.
annotation.definitionFit: Racists are one kind of bigot, people intolerant of others.

entries.clue: And I do it in trouble as well (2,8)

indicatorNotes.trouble: the letters are thrown into trouble, disorder

annotation.surface: A confession that I, too, get into trouble.
annotation.walkthrough: "In trouble" looks like a single phrase, but "in" belongs to the fodder and "trouble" alone is the indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both phrases mean also, adding something further to what came before.

entries.clue: Award writer rejected – what a surprise! (4)

indicatorNotes.rejected: a rejected thing is sent back where it came from, so ME is sent back to front

blocks.note: the writer of a clue refers to themselves as me

annotation.surface: A writer turned down for an award, and the shock of it.
annotation.walkthrough: The writer is the setter, who is ME in crosswords.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the statuette given for achievement in American television is one particular award.

indicatorNotes.about: the film goes round the nothing

annotation.surface: A dull, drippy movie that is about nothing.
annotation.walkthrough: "Wet film" suggests a feeble movie; film here is a thin layer of mist.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: damp describes something wet only slightly, and "rather" does that softening.

entries.clue: Got too big to be caught, maybe? Hopelessly wrong (8)

annotation.definitionNote: OUTGROWN is the past participle, while "Got too big" reads most naturally as a past tense; both work after "has": has outgrown / has got too big.

indicatorNotes.Hopelessly: the letters are hopelessly mixed up

blocks.note: in cricket, being caught is one way for a batsman to be out

annotation.surface: A fish that grew too big to be caught, a hopelessly wrong guess.
annotation.walkthrough: In cricket, a batsman is out when caught; "maybe" flags caught as one example.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for a phrase: clothes a child can no longer wear because the child became too large for them are said to be outgrown.

indicatorNotes.brings up: in a down entry, the letters are brought up, bottom to top

annotation.surface: A letter bringing up the results of a brain scan.
annotation.walkthrough: Gee is the spelled-out name of the letter G.
annotation.definitionFit: A crossword convention: a letter can be defined by its spelled-out name, the way G is written as a word.

indicatorNotes.stops: the cat stops up, plugs, the spies

annotation.surface: A cat foiling returning spies, perhaps with a bomb.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark on "bomb?" signals a definition by example: atomic is what kind of bomb, not a synonym for bomb.
annotation.definitionFit: An atomic bomb; the question mark admits the answer describes the bomb rather than names it.

blocks.note: a pen is a female swan

annotation.surface: Trees that resemble swans.
annotation.walkthrough: A pen is a female swan, and a cob a male one.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: these poplars with trembling leaves are one kind of tree among many.

entries.clue: Bird that’s coming back round initially thanks you forever (8)

indicatorNotes.coming back: the letters for "that's" come back, reversed
indicatorNotes.round: the reversed letters go round the bird
indicatorNotes.initially: take the first letters of the next two words

blocks.note: i.e. stands for id est, that is

annotation.surface: A migrating bird thanking you endlessly on its return.
annotation.walkthrough: "That's" stands for "that is", abbreviated i.e. "Forever" works as a noun here: it took forever, it took an eternity.
annotation.definitionFit: Forever, as a noun, means an endless time, an eternity.
